implementation_notes: The validator crate gives Rust the collected form: derive Validate on the request struct, annotate the fields, and validate() returns Result<(), ValidationErrors> where ValidationErrors holds one entry per failed field (with ValidationErrorsKind for nested structs); nothing throws and no early return is needed. Choose it when the constraints are declarative; use the manual variant when the checks need application state or the error type must be your own.
pitfalls: The ? operator and unwrap() are short-circuiting; inside an accumulating validator every ? silently drops the remaining checks.
ValidationErrors is keyed by field name and cannot carry your own error codes, so map it into the API's Problem type at the boundary.
A field's own attributes stop at that field's first failure; cross-field rules need a custom function on the struct.

variants.name: hand-rolled Vec<Violation> accumulation
variants.implementation_notes: Without the crate the accumulator is a Vec: push a Violation for each failed check and return Err(list) once, or Ok(()) when the vector stayed empty; the stdlib Result documents the outcome in the signature and is #[must_use], so the compiler warns when a caller ignores it. Choose this form when the violations must carry your own codes and severities or when the checks need borrowed application state.
pitfalls: Result<(), Vec<E>> propagates as one value: a caller that maps it away with .ok() or unwrap_or_default() discards the diagnostics.
Using ? inside the function forces the error type to unify with the caller's, which usually means converting the whole vector at the boundary anyway.
Empty versus non-empty is the only invariant; a bug that pushes a placeholder Violation turns a valid input into an error.
